quiz_hp:1.q: In which site does hematopoiesis first occur in the embryo?
quiz_hp:1.r: Primordial stage: yolk sac, large nucleated RBCs.

quiz_hp:11.q: The cell labeled M lies against the wall of a venous sinusoid (VS). What does it push into the sinusoid lumen?
quiz_hp:11.r: Megakaryocyte on the abluminal surface extends proplatelets through the endothelium.
quiz_hp:11.alt: Drawing of red bone marrow with labels VS, HC, RC, AC, VC and M

quiz_hp:15.q: The deep blue cytoplasm of this erythroid precursor reflects a high content of what?
quiz_hp:15.alt: Blood cell with deep blue cytoplasm and a round dark nucleus

quiz_hp:16.q: Which cell will this erythroid precursor become next?
quiz_hp:16.r: Faculty image p. 490 = polychromatophilic erythroblast; next is the normoblast.
quiz_hp:16.alt: Smear with one nucleated cell among red cells

quiz_hp:17.q: What happens next to the nucleus of this cell?
quiz_hp:17.r: Faculty image p. 491 = normoblast (pyknotic eccentric nucleus); nucleus is extruded and eaten by the macrophage.
quiz_hp:17.alt: Smear with one small cell with a dense round nucleus

quiz_hp:18.q: The cells containing a blue network normally make up about what share of circulating red cells?
quiz_hp:18.r: Reticulocytes: about 1% of RBCs; excess may indicate anemia.
quiz_hp:18.alt: Smear with red cells, some containing a blue network

quiz_hp:19.q: The blue network in these cells consists of clumped
quiz_hp:19.r: Supravital stain: ribosomes clump into a blue reticulum.
quiz_hp:19.alt: Smear with red cells, some containing a blue network

quiz_hp:2.q: Which sites dominate hematopoiesis during the second trimester?

quiz_hp:20.q: This is the first recognizable cell of the red cell line. The hormone that drives its progenitors is made mainly in which organ?
quiz_hp:20.r: EPO: about 90% from renal peritubular cells, 10% liver.
quiz_hp:20.alt: Large cell with a large round nucleus and blue cytoplasm

quiz_hp:21.q: Which erythroid stage is the first that can no longer divide?
quiz_hp:21.r: Mitotic: pro, basophilic, polychromatophilic. Postmitotic from the normoblast.

quiz_hp:22.q: This marrow biopsy is packed with uniform immature cells. Which clinical course is expected?
quiz_hp:22.r: Acute leukemia: immature cells, progresses rapidly (pp. 480, 488).
quiz_hp:22.alt: Biopsy packed with small uniform cells

quiz_hp:23.q: This cell is the first in its line to make granules. Which kind are they?
quiz_hp:23.alt: Large cell with many dark granules and a round nucleus

quiz_hp:24.q: This precursor has a round nucleus and has begun making a second type of granule. What can first be determined at this stage?
quiz_hp:24.r: Myelocyte: specific granules; first stage distinguishable as neutrophilic, eosinophilic or basophilic.
quiz_hp:24.alt: Cell with granules and a round eccentric nucleus

quiz_hp:26.q: A rise of this cell type in the blood most strongly suggests which condition?
quiz_hp:26.r: Faculty image p. 492 = band cell; band neutrophil accumulation in blood indicates bacterial infection.
quiz_hp:26.alt: Smear with a cell whose nucleus is horseshoe shaped

quiz_hp:27.q: Which granulocyte precursor contains no specific granules?
quiz_hp:27.r: Faculty question p. 493: promyelocyte has non-specific granules only.

quiz_hp:4.q: From which site is bone marrow usually sampled in a young child?
quiz_hp:4.r: Young children: tibia; adults: pelvis or sternum.

quiz_hp:6.q: Which cell is derived from the lymphoid stem cell line?
quiz_hp:6.r: Lymphoid line: T cells, B cells (and plasma cells); everything else is myeloid.

quiz_hp_b:1.q: A 40-year-old needs a diagnostic marrow sample. Which curve marks sites that are still hematopoietic at that age, and what are they?
quiz_hp_b:1.r: On the fetus-to-adult graph the axial skeleton curve stays high through adult life, while the distal long bones curve falls to zero by about 25 years (p. 450).
quiz_hp_b:1.alt: Graph of hematopoietic activity against age in the fetus and adult, with two adult curves marked X and Y.

quiz_hp_b:10.q: The arrowed cell is far larger than its neighbours in this normal marrow. Which factor is shown driving its lineage on the slides?
quiz_hp_b:10.r: The giant cell is a megakaryocyte; the thrombopoiesis slide labels thrombopoietin (TPO) at the start of the line and the nucleus as polyploid (p. 478, p. 479; image p. 485).
quiz_hp_b:10.alt: Normal bone marrow at high power with an arrow on one very large cell among many small cells.

quiz_hp_b:11.q: Which stage follows this neutrophil precursor, and what nuclear shape will that stage have?
o: Band cell with a horse shoe nucleus
Mature cell with a segmented nucleus
quiz_hp_b:11.r: The cell has a bean shaped nucleus, so it is a metamyelocyte; the next stage is the band cell with a horse shoe shaped nucleus, then the segmented mature cell (p. 470, p. 472; image p. 1158).
quiz_hp_b:11.alt: Smear showing one nucleated cell with an indented nucleus and finely granular cytoplasm, among red cells.

quiz_hp_b:12.q: A lymph node biopsy shows a neoplasm of lymphocytes containing giant Reed-Sternberg cells. How is it classified on the slide?
quiz_hp_b:12.r: Lymphomas are neoplasms of lymphocytes, and Hodgkin's disease is the one characterized by giant Reed-Sternberg cells (p. 480).

quiz_hp_b:13.q: A myelogenous leukemia consists of more mature cells and runs a less aggressive course. Which target of Gleevec doubled five-year survival in this form?
quiz_hp_b:13.r: More mature cells and a less aggressive course define the chronic form; Gleevec targets the BCR-Abl tyrosine kinase and raised five-year survival from 31% to 59% (p. 481).

quiz_hp_b:14.q: Two marrow biopsies are shown at the same low power. Which one is acute leukemia, and why?
o: B, immature cells replace the marrow
A, fat cells replace the marrow
B, fat cells replace the marrow
A, immature cells replace the marrow
quiz_hp_b:14.r: Normal marrow is pale and speckled with fat spaces (p. 484); in acute leukemia tumor cells replace the normal hematopoietic tissue, so the marrow is solidly packed with cells (p. 487, p. 481).
quiz_hp_b:14.alt: Two low-power bone marrow biopsies side by side, labelled A and B; one is densely purple and one is pale and lacy.

quiz_hp_b:2.q: A marrow toxin destroys myeloid stem cells but spares lymphoid stem cells. Which pair of products can no longer be made?
quiz_hp_b:2.r: Myeloid stem cells give erythrocytes, megakaryocytes (whose fragments are platelets), granulocytes and monocytes; lymphoid stem cells give T and B lymphocytes (p. 453).

quiz_hp_b:3.q: On the lecture's table of trends, a cell has lost its potentiality and self-renewing capacity but is at its peak of mitotic activity. Which class of cell is it?
quiz_hp_b:3.r: In the trends table potentiality and self-renewing capacity taper out by the end of the progenitor column, while mitotic activity is widest in the precursor (blast) column and is gone in mature cells (p. 454).

quiz_hp_b:4.q: Large empty-looking cells dominate this marrow. What is this marrow called, and in whom is it typical on the slide?
quiz_hp_b:4.r: The slide pairs red marrow with hematogenous (young) and yellow marrow with adipose cells (older); the big empty cells are adipose cells (p. 455).
quiz_hp_b:4.alt: Line drawing of bone marrow in which large round empty cells take up most of the field.

quiz_hp_b:5.q: The arrowed branching cell forms a network between the marrow sinusoids. What does the slide call the role of this cell?
o: Fat storage of the yellow marrow
quiz_hp_b:5.r: The red label on the slide reads Stromal Cell (Hematopoietic Inductive Microenvironment); proplatelets come from megakaryocytes, nuclei are engulfed by macrophages and the lining is endothelium (p. 457, p. 458).
quiz_hp_b:5.alt: Line drawing of marrow with the blood-forming cells washed out, an arrow on a branching cell between wide vascular channels.

quiz_hp_b:6.q: Developing red cells surround the arrowed central cell. What does this cell do for them, according to the slides?
quiz_hp_b:6.r: The central cell of an erythroblastic island is a macrophage (p. 465), and the marrow structure slide says the macrophage engulfs nuclei extruded from orthochromatic erythroblasts (p. 458).
quiz_hp_b:6.alt: Drawing of a ring of developing cells around one large central cell, which is marked by an arrow.

quiz_hp_b:7.q: Erythroid precursors mature from left to right on this graph. What do the falling yellow curve and the rising red curve represent?
quiz_hp_b:7.r: As the erythroid line matures RNA falls and hemoglobin rises; the stages slide shows the same trend with cell size shrinking (p. 463, p. 462).
quiz_hp_b:7.alt: Graph of concentration against maturation with a falling yellow curve and a rising red curve.

quiz_hp_b:8.q: Judge this marrow cell by the shape of its nucleus and the colour of its granules. Which precursor is it?
quiz_hp_b:8.r: A bean shaped nucleus marks a metamyelocyte and the specific granules name the type, here large red eosinophilic granules (p. 1158; shapes on p. 470).
quiz_hp_b:8.alt: Smear showing one nucleated cell with an indented nucleus and cytoplasm packed with granules, among red cells.

quiz_hp_b:9.q: Kupffer cells, osteoclasts and Langerhans cells all arise from one type of blood cell. Which marrow cell directly precedes that blood cell?
quiz_hp_b:9.r: The mononuclear phagocyte system slide runs CFU-GM, monoblast, promonocyte, monocyte, tissue macrophage, and lists Kupffer cells, osteoclasts and Langerhans cells among the tissue macrophages (p. 476).

Hematopoiesis High-Yield Tables (Exam 3)

Hematopoiesis (Djakiew) was 15/30 on your September quiz, with granulopoiesis at 0/4. Page numbers are pages of the combined PDF: slides pp. 446–494, handout pp. 495–507. Everything is from those pages unless labeled (outside the slides).

1. Where blood is made, fetus to adult (LO 1)

Hematopoiesis moves through three sites before birth and ends in the bone marrow, which is the only site at term (pp. 450, 495).

Stage Site When it dominates What it makes
Primordial Yolk sac Earliest embryo Large, nucleated red cells (primordial erythroblasts)
Hepato-spleno-thymic Liver, spleen, thymus Second trimester Granulocyte and megakaryocyte precursors; definitive erythroblasts
Medullo-lymphatic Bone marrow and lymph nodes Third trimester; exclusive at term All cell types

Extramedullary hematopoiesis is the return of blood production to the liver and spleen after prolonged, severe demand in a child or adult (p. 495).

Age Red marrow Page
At birth Every bone cavity, completely full of cells 497
Adult Only 50% of marrow is active 497
Adult sites Ribs, sternum, pelvis; proximal quarter of humerus and femur 497
On the slide's curve Axial skeleton stays active; distal long bones fall off by about age 20 450
Marrow type Looks Activity Page
Red Hematogenous tissue; highly vascular, soft Active (young) 455, 497
Yellow Adipose cells and connective tissue Inactive (older) 455, 499

Red and yellow marrow are interconvertible as demand changes (p. 499).

Patient Where marrow is sampled Page
Young child Shaft of the tibia 452, 499
Adult Pelvis (iliac spines) or sternum 452, 499

The slide also marks the spinous processes of the vertebrae as a site (p. 452).

2. Stem cells and the two branches (LO 2)

One pluripotential stem cell makes every blood cell, and its first split is into a myeloid line and a lymphoid line (pp. 453, 495).

Branch Stays or leaves Makes Page
Myeloid Develops in the bone marrow Erythrocytes, megakaryocytes and platelets, granulocytes (neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil), monocytes 453, 501
Lymphoid Generally migrates to lymphoid organs T lymphocytes (cellular immunity), B lymphocytes (humoral immunity) 453, 501

Monocytes that leave the blood become macrophages (p. 453).

Pluripotential stem cell fact Detail Page
Other name Hemocytoblast 453
Appearance No distinguishing features 499
Markers CD34 positive; also carries the c-kit receptor 501
How common 0.01% of nucleated marrow cells 499
Reserve 5% of normal stem cells can repopulate the whole marrow 499
Cell cycle Most are not dividing, which protects them from depletion 501
Where else Small numbers in blood; large numbers in umbilical cord blood 501
Restricted stem cell Makes Page
BFU-E (burst forming unit, erythroid) Red cells; needs high erythropoietin 503
CFU-E (colony forming unit, erythroid) Red cells; responds to low erythropoietin and proliferates faster 503
CFU-GM Neutrophils and macrophages (monocytes) 503, 505
CFU-Eo Eosinophils 503
CFU-Bas Basophils 503
CFU-Meg Megakaryocytes and platelets 505
Growth factor Made by Acts on Page
Erythropoietin (EPO) Kidney peritubular cells, about 90%; liver, 10% Erythroid progenitors 461, 501
Thrombopoietin (TPO) Liver, bone marrow and other tissues Megakaryocyte maturation, size and number 478, 505
GM-CSF (granulocyte/macrophage colony stimulating factor) Granulocyte and macrophage colonies 503
Stem cell factors Bone marrow stromal cells Stem cell survival; without them stem cells die by apoptosis 495
As cells mature Trend (p. 454)
Potentiality Falls
Self-renewing capacity Falls
Mitotic activity Highest in progenitors and precursors, then lost
Typical morphology Appears in precursors (blasts)
Functional activity Appears in mature cells

The slide writes "Leukemias, Lymphomas" under the progenitor and precursor columns of that table (p. 454).

3. Bone marrow structure (LO 3)

Marrow has a vascular compartment of sinusoids and an extravascular hematopoietic compartment between them (p. 497).

Part What it is Page
Endosteum The outer capsule of the marrow 497
Venous sinusoids Thin-walled; continuous endothelium with a discontinuous basement membrane 497
Stromal cells (adventitial reticular cells) Framework of cells plus reticular fibers; cover the outer surface of the sinusoid 457, 497
Hematopoietic inductive microenvironment Stromal cells, adhesion molecules and growth factors; directs differentiation and release 495, 497
Macrophages Remove debris and dead cells 499

Stem cells are "seeds in the soil": they need that microenvironment to develop, and they can home back to it (pp. 495, 497).

Lineage Where it sits (handout) How it reaches the blood Page
Erythroid Near the sinuses, around a nurse macrophage (erythroblastic islet) Passes through the endothelium 498
Granulocytes Away from the sinuses Motile metamyelocytes move toward the sinus 498
Megakaryocytes On the outer (adventitial) surface of the sinus Push proplatelets through the endothelium into the lumen 499, 507
Lymphocytes B cells mature in marrow; T cells mature in the thymus 499

One conflict to know about: the textbook figure on slide 458 says developing granulocytes are found adjacent to venous sinusoids, while his handout says granulopoiesis is found away from the sinuses. The handout is his own wording, so answer "away from the sinuses" unless a question quotes the figure.

Marrow function Page
Production of blood cells 499
Destruction of erythrocytes 499
Iron storage, from hemoglobin breakdown 499
Central organ for B lymphocyte development 499

Aplastic anemia is pancytopenia with a fatty, "empty", hypocellular marrow (p. 499).

4. Erythropoiesis (LO 3)

Across the red cell line the cell shrinks, the cytoplasm goes from blue to pink, and the nucleus condenses and is thrown out (pp. 462, 1154).

Stage Cytoplasm Nucleus Mitotic How to spot it
Proerythroblast Basophilic Homogeneous chromatin Yes Largest; first recognizable erythroid cell
Basophilic erythroblast Basophilic; RNA-rich for protein synthesis Checkerboard heterochromatin Yes Deep blue rim around a checkerboard nucleus
Polychromatophilic erythroblast Basophilic and eosinophilic together Yes Gray or mixed-color cytoplasm
Orthochromatophilic erythroblast (normoblast) Eosinophilic Condensed (pyknotic), eccentric No Small dark off-center nucleus; cell about red-cell size
Reticulocyte Residual RNA None No Blue web with a supravital stain
Erythrocyte Uniform eosinophilic None No

The descriptions come from his review lecture (p. 1154), the faculty answer on p. 491, and the handout list (p. 503). "Gray" and "deep blue rim" are my wording for the same facts.

Trend through the line Direction Page
Cell size Falls: 500+ fL to about 90 fL 462
RNA and mitochondria Fall 462–463
Hemoglobin Rises from 0 462–463
Start of hemoglobin synthesis As the basophilic erythroblast becomes polychromatophilic 465
Divisions 3 mitotic divisions, all before the normoblast 465, 503
Timing Slide or handout Page
Whole maturation 7 days 503
Around the erythroblastic island 5 days 465
Reticulocyte About 3 days to mature 463
Red cell in blood 120+ days 462
Reticulocyte fact Detail Page
Nucleus Extruded by the normoblast and eaten by the nurse macrophage 458, 503
Stain Supravital stain, such as brilliant cresyl blue; ribosomes clump into a blue "reticulum" 467, 503
With ordinary stains Called a polychromatophilic erythrocyte 503
Still makes The final 20% of hemoglobin, and cytoskeleton 503
Normal count About 1% of red cells in blood 467
High count May indicate anemia 467
Erythropoietin fact Detail Page
Sensor and source Renal interstitial peritubular cells detect low blood oxygen and secrete it 461
Share Kidney about 90%, liver 10% 501
Action Drives proliferation and differentiation of erythroid progenitors and prevents their apoptosis 461
Result More reticulocytes enter the blood; oxygen delivery rises 461
Clinical Recombinant erythropoietin cut transfusion need in renal dialysis by 70–80% 501

5. Granulopoiesis (LO 3)

Two things change down the granulocyte line: which granules are being made, and the shape of the nucleus (pp. 469–472, 505, 1155).

Stage Granules Nucleus Mitotic Amoeboid movement
Myeloblast None Round Yes No
Promyelocyte Azurophilic (non-specific, primary) granules first made Round or oval Yes No
Myelocyte Specific (secondary) granules first made Round or oval, often eccentric Yes No
Metamyelocyte No new granules; holds both kinds Bean shaped No Begins
Band (stab) cell Both kinds Horseshoe shaped No Yes
Mature granulocyte Both kinds Segmented No Yes

Non-specific granules are lysosomes (p. 1155).

"First" question Answer Page
First cell with any granules Promyelocyte 469, 505
First cell with specific granules Myelocyte 469, 505
First stage you can call neutrophilic, eosinophilic or basophilic Myelocyte 505
First stage with amoeboid movement Metamyelocyte 505
First stage where the nucleus indents (lobulation begins) Metamyelocyte 469
Last stage that divides Myelocyte 505
Golgi through the line Detail (p. 471)
Promyelocyte Developed Golgi making azurophilic granules
Myelocyte Developed Golgi making specific granules
Metamyelocyte Atrophic Golgi; abundant specific granules, few azurophilic
Timing Value Page
Mitotic phase in marrow 7.5 days 470
Post-mitotic phase in marrow 6.5 days 470
Time in blood Half-life about 6 hours 470
Time in tissues About 1–2 days 470
Marrow reserve Most neutrophils sit in the marrow about 4 days, ready for rapid release 505

The slide adds up to 14 days of marrow development, while the handout says maturation takes 11 days (pp. 470, 505). Know both numbers.

Band neutrophils accumulating in the blood indicate bacterial infection (p. 474). Recombinant GM-CSF helps patients with a low white cell count after marrow transplant, cancer therapy, AIDS or aplastic anemia (p. 503).

6. Monocytes and platelets (LO 3)

Monocytes share a stem cell with neutrophils, and platelets are fragments of the largest cell in the marrow (pp. 476, 505).

Monocyte stage Detail Page
CFU-GM Shared restricted stem cell 505
Monoblast Virtually identical to a myeloblast 505
Promonocyte First morphologically identifiable cell 505
Monocyte About 6 days in marrow, then a blood half-time of 1–3 days 476
Tissue macrophage Lives for months 476

The mononuclear phagocyte system is the macrophages, their precursors and their specialized descendants (p. 505).

Tissue Macrophage name (p. 476)
Liver Kupffer cell
Lung Interstitial and alveolar macrophages
Bone Osteoclast
Brain Reactive microglial cell
Epidermis Langerhans cell
Granuloma Multinucleated giant cell
Serous cavities Pleural and peritoneal macrophages
Platelet line Detail Page
Megakaryoblast Giant polyploid nucleus made by endomitosis: the nucleus duplicates without the cell dividing 479, 505
Megakaryocyte Largest cell in the marrow, about 100 microns; lobulated nucleus, 2n to 64n 478, 505
Position Outer (abluminal) surface of the sinusoid 507
Proplatelets Cytoplasmic pseudopods pushed through the endothelium into the sinusoid lumen 458, 507
Platelet Bits of cytoplasm pinched off along platelet demarcation channels 507
Outside the marrow Some megakaryocytes reach the lung's vascular bed and finish making platelets there 507

Thrombopoietin regulates the maturation, size and number of megakaryocytes (p. 505).

7. Leukemia, lymphoma and the marrow biopsy

Leukemia is tested for with a bone marrow biopsy (p. 483).

Term Definition Page
Lymphoma Neoplasm of lymphocytes 480
Hodgkin's disease Marked by giant Reed-Sternberg cells; 5 subtypes 480
Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma 12 B-cell types and 12 T-cell types 480
Leukemia Neoplasm of leukocytes and their precursors 480
Myelogenous leukemia Primarily involves bone marrow; classified by precursor cell type 481
Feature Acute leukemia Chronic leukemia
Cells Immature More mature
Course Rapid progression Less aggressive
Leukemia fact Detail Page
Origin Clonal expansion of immature lymphoid or myeloid progenitors blocked at one stage of differentiation 499
Effect on marrow Tumor cells replace normal hematopoietic tissue 481
Gleevec Targets the BCR-Abl tyrosine kinase in chronic myelogenous leukemia; 5-year survival rose from 31% to 59% 481
Biopsy What you see Page
Normal marrow Mixed cell types with fat spaces between bone trabeculae; megakaryocytes present 484–485
Acute leukemia Marrow packed with sheets of uniform immature cells; fat spaces crowded out 487–488

The biopsy descriptions are mine from his images; the slides give only the titles.

8. Faculty questions on the slides, and your September misses

The five practice questions at the end are faculty-written, and three of them ask what comes before the cell shown (pp. 489–493). Learn each line as an ordered list, not as separate pictures.

Slide What it asked Answer on the slide
489 Which cell is not from a myeloid progenitor Lymphocyte
490 Which cell precedes the one shown (a polychromatophilic erythroblast) Basophilic erythroblast
491 Identify the cell from erythropoiesis Normoblast: pyknotic, eccentric nucleus; cell about red-cell size
492 Which cell precedes the one shown (a band cell) Metamyelocyte
493 Which cell does not contain specific granules Promyelocyte

The review lecture adds two more: a polychromatophilic erythroblast identified by its polychromatophilia (p. 1172), and a metamyelocyte identified by its kidney-bean nucleus (p. 1173).

The two orders to say out loud:

  1. Proerythroblast, basophilic erythroblast, polychromatophilic erythroblast, normoblast, reticulocyte, erythrocyte
  2. Myeloblast, promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, band cell, mature granulocyte
Area The fact you missed in September Page
Granulopoiesis The promyelocyte first makes azurophilic granules 505
Granulopoiesis The myelocyte is the first stage distinguishable by lineage 505
Granulopoiesis Amoeboid movement begins at the metamyelocyte 505
Granulopoiesis Band neutrophils in blood indicate bacterial infection 474
Erythropoiesis Basophilic erythroblast cytoplasm is RNA-rich (free ribosomes) 465
Erythropoiesis Erythroblastic islets sit next to the sinuses 498
Erythropoiesis Excess reticulocytes signal anemia 467
Erythropoiesis About 90% of erythropoietin comes from renal peritubular cells 501
Development The yolk sac makes large nucleated red cells 495
Development Liver and spleen dominate in the second trimester 495
Marrow Yellow marrow can revert to red 499
Marrow Sinusoids have continuous endothelium with a discontinuous basal lamina 497
Marrow Proplatelets cross the sinus wall into the lumen 507
Disease Leukemias arise from immature progenitors blocked in maturation 499
Disease Sheets of immature blasts mean acute leukemia with a rapid course 480, 488

From the review quiz you also missed erythroid stage identification five times out of six: proerythroblast, basophilic, polychromatophilic and orthochromatophilic erythroblasts. Section 4's first table is the fix.
